Package org.apache.juneau.rest.server.filter

Class RequestBoundaryFilter

java.lang.Object
org.apache.juneau.rest.server.filter.RequestBoundaryFilter
All Implemented Interfaces:
jakarta.servlet.Filter
Direct Known Subclasses:
LoopbackBoundaryFilter
public class RequestBoundaryFilter extends Object implements jakarta.servlet.Filter
Applies a RequestBoundary to every request reaching the servlet container, rejecting those that did not come from a page this application served.
Why a servlet filter, and not a mixin or a guard

The boundary's value depends entirely on there being no way around it, and the two lighter-weight Juneau mechanisms both leave one:

  • A RestGuard is declared per resource or per operation, so an endpoint added later is unprotected until someone remembers to declare it — and its omission is invisible in review, because nothing about the new endpoint looks different.
  • A mixin's @RestStartCall hook fires only for requests that resolved to one of that mixin's own endpoints, so a boundary packaged that way would not see the host resource's operations at all.

A filter registered at /* sees every request the container handles: every Juneau resource and mixin, static resources served by the container or by another framework in the same application, and the paths that resolve to nothing and would 404. Nothing can opt out by omission, which is the property that makes it worth having.

Rejection behavior

A rejected request is answered directly and the chain is not invoked, so the request never reaches application code. The response carries the boundary's chosen status, a "X-Request-Boundary" header naming the reason, Cache-Control: no-store, and a small JSON body carrying the same reason and a message.

A rejection is never rendered as an empty result or a silent no-op. A security refusal that looks like "no data" teaches the user to ignore it, and the point of answering explicitly is that a genuine misconfiguration — the application being reached at localhost when it accepts 127.0.0.1, say — is immediately diagnosable instead of presenting as an inexplicably broken page.

Token availability to the page renderer

On an allowed request the boundary's token for that request is placed under the TOKEN_ATTRIBUTE request attribute, and the header name it must be sent back under is placed under the HEADER_ATTRIBUTE sibling attribute, so a page-rendering endpoint can embed both without needing its own reference to the boundary.

A page that embeds the token in more than one place should give each place its own value: a CsrfBoundary masks its token under a fresh pad on every call, so the secret never repeats in the page. For that the filter also places a Supplier<String> under TOKEN_SUPPLIER_ATTRIBUTE; each get() returns a new value. Read it from the servlet request and test it with instanceof TokenSupplier: converting the attribute to a string yields the supplier's own description, not a token. TOKEN_ATTRIBUTE keeps a single value for renderers that read only a string.

A response that embeds the token must not be cached, or a cache hands the token to whoever asks next. The code that writes the token calls markTokenBearing(HttpServletResponse) before it writes any of the body; this filter cannot know which responses embed it.

Sessions

A CsrfBoundary with a per-session token needs the session to exist before the page is written, or the page carries a token that verifies against nothing. The boundary itself never creates one; this filter does, with getSession(true), and only when all of these hold:

  • CsrfBoundary.createSessions() is on (the default);
  • the request is allowed and its effective method is safe;
  • the request looks like a page load: Sec-Fetch-Mode: navigate or Sec-Fetch-Dest: document or iframe; or, with no Sec-Fetch-* header at all, an Accept header naming text/html.

So a curl GET with Accept: */* never creates a session, while a client that asks for HTML, Juneau's own HTML REST pages included, does. The filter never changes a session id and never sets cookie attributes; those stay the application's (see CsrfBoundary).

Registration: order and dispatcher types

Map the filter at /* so nothing can be reached around it. Register it ahead of any filter that acts on the request on the application's behalf. A CsrfBoundary using CONTAINER is the exception that must come after one filter: the container's forwarded-header rewrite, when that is a filter (Spring Boot's ForwardedHeaderFilter sits at Ordered.HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE, so register this one strictly later).

The filter judges every request it is handed, whatever its DispatcherType; it has no dispatch-type check of its own, so which dispatches it sees is decided entirely by the registration. Register it for REQUEST only unless there is a reason to do otherwise:

  • an ERROR dispatch of a refused or failed write may arrive without the token header and be refused in turn, replacing the error page with a 403;
  • a FORWARD to an HTML view looks like a page load and can create a session.

ASYNC, ERROR and FORWARD are opt-in. A container's default registration (a null dispatcher set in addMappingForUrlPatterns, or Spring Boot's FilterRegistrationBean default) is REQUEST only.

Example (Spring Boot):

@Bean public FilterRegistrationBean<RequestBoundaryFilter> boundary(RequestBoundary b) { var reg = new FilterRegistrationBean<>(new RequestBoundaryFilter(b)); reg.addUrlPatterns("/*"); reg.setOrder(Ordered.HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE); return reg; }

    • HEADER_ATTRIBUTE

      public static final String HEADER_ATTRIBUTE
      Request attribute under which an allowed request carries the boundary's CSRF header name (RequestBoundary.csrfHeader()).

      Published as a sibling of TOKEN_ATTRIBUTE on the same allowed-request path so a page-rendering document shell (e.g. the console <@console> FTL directive) can emit both the csrf-token meta value and the header name the client script must send it back under, without needing its own reference to the boundary.

      See Also:
      • Constant Field Values

    • TOKEN_SUPPLIER_ATTRIBUTE

      public static final String TOKEN_SUPPLIER_ATTRIBUTE
      Request attribute under which an allowed request carries a Supplier<String> of CSRF token values, one per get().

      Each value is RequestBoundary.tokenFor(HttpServletRequest) called afresh, so a masking boundary gives every embed in a page its own pad. Read the attribute from the servlet request and check it with instanceof TokenSupplier; never convert it to a string.

      Request code can call setAttribute on this name, so a reader must trust the value only when it is a RequestBoundaryFilter.TokenSupplier, a type only this filter can create. A value of any other type under this name was put there by someone else: treat it as "no token" and fail closed, rather than embed what it returns.

      See Also:

    • markTokenBearing

      public static void markTokenBearing(jakarta.servlet.http.HttpServletResponse res)
      Marks a response that embeds a CSRF token as one no cache may store.

      Sets Cache-Control: private, no-store, replacing any value already set, so an earlier public, max-age=... cannot survive alongside it. Call it before the first byte of the body is written: once the response is committed, headers can no longer change.

      Parameters:
      res - The response. Must not be null.
